title: The Peacock and the Snake
devanagari: अस्ति स्तम्भतले बिलं तदुपरि क्रीडाशिखण्डी स्थितः
क्षिप्रं ब्रूहि तयोर्बिलात् कतिकरैः साम्येन गत्योर्युतिः॥
translation: There is a hole at the foot of a pillar, and on top of it stands a pet peacock. The pillar is nine hastas high. Seeing a snake coming toward the hole from a distance of three times the pillar's height, the peacock swoops down on it slantwise. Say quickly: at how many hastas from the hole do they meet, if their speeds are equal?
translation_hi: एक खंभे के नीचे एक बिल है और खंभे के ऊपर एक पालतू मोर बैठा है। खंभा नौ हाथ ऊँचा है। खंभे की ऊँचाई के तीन गुना दूरी से एक साँप को बिल की ओर आते देखकर मोर तिरछा उस पर झपटता है। जल्दी बताओ, यदि दोनों की गति बराबर हो, तो बिल से कितने हाथ की दूरी पर दोनों मिलते हैं?

words.meaning: at the foot of a pillar

words.note: nava + ucchrita: अ + उ → ओ (guna sandhi).
Gerund of √drish. The -tva ending means 'having done'.
Oblique, diagonal. Today: तिर्यक् रेखा = oblique line.
Adverb. The mathematician is told to answer fast!
Genitive dual of tad. Visarga → र् before a voiced sound.
kati = how many; kara = hand, used as the hasta unit. Instrumental plural.
Instrumental of samya: 'their speeds being equal'.

grammar: Guna sandhi: नव + उच्छ्रिते → नवोच्छ्रिते and तस्य + उपरि → तस्योपरि. अ + उ always becomes ओ.
Long vowel sandhi: दृष्ट्वा + अहिम् → दृष्ट्वाहिम्. Two similar vowels merge into one long vowel.
Dual number: Sanskrit has singular, dual and plural. तयोः and गत्योः are dual because there are exactly two animals.
Ablative case: बिलात् = 'from the hole'. The distance is measured from the hole, which tells you exactly what x is in the equation.
Gerund: दृष्ट्वा 'having seen'. Very common: गत्वा (having gone), कृत्वा (having done).
question: How many hastas from the hole do they meet?
solution:
Let the meeting point be x hastas from the hole. The snake travels 27 − x. The peacock flies the hypotenuse √(9² + x²).

Equal speeds and equal time mean equal distances: √(81 + x²) = 27 − x

81 + x² = 729 − 54x + x²  ⟹  54x = 648  ⟹  x = 12 hastas

Bhaskara's own rule (verse 151): x = ½ (d − h²/d) = ½ (27 − 81/27) = ½ (24) = 12

Science link: both animals travel 15 hastas, giving the right triangle 9, 12, 15. That is the 3, 4, 5 triangle scaled by 3. Bhaskara uses the Pythagorean theorem (भुजकोटिकर्णन्याय, the base-upright-hypotenuse rule) here.
